response:
Retrieval-augmented generation systems maintain a vector index that is rarely static — documents are added, updated, or deleted on rolling schedules, while the embedding model itself may be fine-tuned or swapped entirely, and these two timelines almost never align. The central question is: how does the distribution of cosine similarity scores between queries and indexed documents degrade as a function of encoder version skew, index staleness, and document corpus drift — and at what point does this degradation silently corrupt retrieval precision before any downstream metric catches it? The key concepts are embedding drift (the shift in geometric position of a fixed document's representation when re-encoded by a newer model), stale vector staleness propagation (the compounding effect when a subset of index vectors are stale while others are fresh, creating a mixed-manifold index), and score distribution skew (the systematic distortion of the cosine similarity landscape that emerges from this mixed manifold, biasing retrieval toward either stale or fresh vectors depending on which subspace the query encoder maps to). A beginner assumes that re-encoding only the "changed" documents is safe and sufficient — the expert knows that even documents with identical text will shift in embedding space after an encoder update, meaning unchanged documents that were never re-indexed become the contamination source, not the updated ones. The deeper worry is that score distribution skew is not uniform across query types: queries that happen to land near the centroid of the stale subspace will retrieve with artificially inflated similarity scores, producing high-confidence retrievals that are semantically incorrect relative to the current encoder's geometry, and these failures are nearly invisible to recall-at-K metrics computed without a ground-truth re-index.

The determining geometric property is the angular displacement between the two encoder manifolds' mean vectors and the spread (isotropy) of each manifold — specifically, if v2 produces embeddings whose centroid is rotated relative to v1's centroid in the shared ambient space, queries encoded by v2 will have systematically higher cosine similarity to v2-encoded documents and lower to v1-encoded ones, producing false negatives for stale (v1) vectors; conversely, if v2 collapses variance (higher anisotropy, as documented in Ethayarajh 2019 for later BERT layers), stale v1 vectors may cluster near query projections by geometric accident, producing false positives. The critical quantity is the Fréchet distance between the two embedding distributions — if the v1 and v2 manifolds are well-separated (large Fréchet distance, e.g., cross-encoder families like GTE vs. E5), false negatives dominate; if they are nearby but differentially anisotropic (same model fine-tuned on new data, small Fréchet distance), false positives dominate because stale vectors occupy a dense cluster that queries still intersect. Empirically, you can detect the failure mode by probing the score gap distribution: for a held-out query set, retrieve top-K and record the fraction of returned documents whose provenance is v1 vs. v2 — under a healthy index this fraction tracks the corpus mix ratio, but a false-positive regime shows v1 over-representation while false-negative shows v1 under-representation relative to that baseline. A sharper signal comes from sentinel pairs: inject known-identical documents encoded by both v1 and v2, then measure the cosine similarity between them — values well below 1.0 (in practice, cross-version similarity for even minor fine-tunes of E5-large drops to 0.7–0.85 on BEIR corpora) quantify the manifold separation and predict which failure mode is active. Production systems like Weaviate and Qdrant expose per-vector metadata that makes the v1/v2 provenance tag tractable, but almost no team instruments this by default, which is precisely why the failure accrues silently.

The theoretical justification for a linear adapter rests on the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma and the empirical near-linearity of encoder representation spaces: if v1 and v2 are both trained with contrastive objectives on overlapping data, their embedding manifolds tend to be related by an approximate affine transformation, meaning a learned orthogonal or linear map W such that Wv1 ≈ v2 can recover most of the geometric structure without re-encoding — this is the same intuition behind MUSE cross-lingual alignment (Conneau et al. 2018) and the Procrustes alignment used in multilingual embedding work, where a closed-form orthogonal solution minimizes ‖WV1 − V2‖_F on anchor pairs. The adapter is justified precisely when the two manifolds are related by a low-rank linear transformation, which holds approximately when v2 is a fine-tune of v1 on in-domain data (rank of the update matrix is bounded, as shown in LoRA's analysis of weight update spectra), but begins to fail when v2 represents an architectural change or drastically different pretraining mixture. The alignment provably fails to close the score gap under three conditions: first, when the intrinsic dimensionality of v1 and v2 manifolds differ — a linear map cannot change the rank of the image, so if v2 encodes richer subspace structure (higher effective rank), projected v1 vectors will be confined to a lower-dimensional subspace and systematically miss v2-native query directions; second, when the corpus contains domain-shifted documents whose v1 representations lie in regions poorly covered by the anchor pairs used to fit W, causing the adapter to extrapolate badly (this is the out-of-support failure mode, measurable as high residual ‖Wv1 − v2‖ on a held-out anchor set); third, when v2 uses a different normalization geometry — for instance, matryoshka representation learning (MRL, Kusupati et al. 2022) truncates to nested subspaces, and a full-dimensional linear map from v1 cannot replicate the nested isotropy structure that makes MRL's truncated similarity scores calibrated. Empirically, BEIR benchmarks show that even well-fitted Procrustes adapters between E5-base and E5-large recover only 60–75% of the nDCG gap relative to full re-encoding on out-of-domain corpora, with the worst failures concentrated in corpora with high lexical-semantic mismatch (TREC-COVID, FiQA) where anchor pair coverage is sparse.

The core partitioning strategy is to tag each v1 vector at index time with a geometric trust score defined as its distance to the nearest anchor point used to fit the adapter — specifically, compute the residual ‖Wv1_i − v2_i‖₂ for all anchor pairs, fit a threshold at the 90th percentile of anchor residuals, then for every non-anchor v1 vector compute its distance to the anchor convex hull (approximated cheaply via k-nearest anchors) and mark it "trusted" if that distance falls below the threshold; this is analogous to the support estimation used in conformal prediction and shares its coverage guarantees when anchors are i.i.d. from the corpus distribution. At query time, route via a two-branch retrieval: encode the query with v2, retrieve candidates from the v2-native partition directly, then for the v1 partition apply the adapter to the query (not the documents, which is cheaper and avoids modifying the index) and retrieve only from trusted v1 vectors, merging ranked lists via reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) or a learned score normalizer calibrated on a small validation set. The trust boundary can be computed without ground-truth labels by treating it as an anomaly detection problem over the anchor residual distribution — a lightweight one-class SVM or isolation forest trained on anchor residuals flags v1 vectors whose adapter projection is geometrically unreliable, and the false-positive rate of this detector is controllable via the contamination hyperparameter, giving a precision-recall tradeoff on retrieval coverage vs. safety. A sharper unsupervised signal is query-side consistency: for a given query, if the top-K from the trusted v1 partition and the v2 partition have low rank overlap (Kendall τ below ~0.3), this flags a distributional mismatch suggesting the query lands outside the adapter's support, and the system can fall back to v2-only retrieval or trigger a background re-encode job for that document cluster. Systems like Qdrant's payload-filtered search and Vespa's two-phase ranking make this partitioned retrieval architecturally tractable with sub-millisecond routing overhead, but the trust scoring must be precomputed at index ingestion time — retrofitting it to an existing index requires a full scan, which is exactly the operational cost teams avoid by not doing full re-encodes in the first place, creating a bootstrapping tension at the heart of the problem.

The assumption that must hold is score exchangeability across partitions: the marginal distributions of cosine similarity scores for relevant documents must be identical (or at least have the same location and scale parameters) in both the v1-adapted and v2-native partitions, so that a score of 0.82 from the v1 partition and 0.82 from the v2 partition represent equivalent degrees of semantic match relative to the query. RRF sidesteps raw score magnitudes by operating on ranks, which makes it more robust to scale differences, but it implicitly assumes rank-order calibration — that the probability of relevance given rank k is the same across partitions; when v2-native vectors are denser and more anisotropic than adapted v1 vectors, v2 scores compress into a narrower high-similarity band, meaning v2 documents systematically occupy lower rank positions (higher rank numbers) than their true relevance warrants, and RRF then under-weights them. The specific retrieval artifact this produces is partition dominance: the final merged top-K becomes disproportionately populated by one partition, not because those documents are more relevant but because their score or rank distribution stochastically dominates — in practice, when v2 embeddings are more anisotropic (as is typical after fine-tuning on hard negatives, e.g., E5-mistral vs. E5-base), the v1-adapted partition produces a wider, flatter score distribution that generates more "mid-tier" ranks, flooding the RRF-merged list with v1 documents and starving the result set of v2-native retrievals. Score normalization approaches like min-max or z-score normalization fail differently: they assume the within-partition score range is comparable across partitions, but if the v1-adapted partition has higher score variance (which it does when adapter residuals are large), z-score normalization over-inflates v1 scores relative to v2, producing a phantom precision inflation where the system reports high similarity scores for documents that the v2 encoder would have ranked much lower on a clean index. The correct mitigation — used in some multi-encoder fusion work like Luan et al.'s CITADEL — is to fit a Platt scaling or isotonic regression calibrator per partition on a small labeled or pseudo-labeled set, transforming raw scores into probability-of-relevance estimates before merging, which requires the calibration data to cover both partitions' score ranges but eliminates the exchangeability assumption by grounding comparison in a common probability scale.

The most reliable real-time observable is the partition provenance ratio in the top-K: compute the fraction of v1-adapted vs. v2-native documents in the merged top-K and compare it against the baseline corpus mix ratio — a statistically significant deviation (detectable via a simple binomial test with the corpus mix as the null proportion) flags partition dominance without any relevance signal, and empirically a deviation exceeding 2× the expected fraction is a robust threshold given typical corpus mix ratios of 30–70% stale. A sharper signal is the inter-partition score gap: for the top-K results, compute the mean cosine similarity of v1-adapted retrievals minus mean cosine similarity of v2-native retrievals — under exchangeability this should be near zero, but partition dominance by v1 produces a positive gap (v1 scores are inflated) while v2 dominance produces a negative gap; this statistic is cheap (two means over K numbers) and can be thresholded at ±0.05 based on calibration data without labels. A complementary observable exploiting query geometry is within-query score variance stratified by partition: if the v1-adapted partition exhibits significantly higher score variance than the v2-native partition for the same query (testable via Levene's test or simply the ratio of within-partition standard deviations), this directly fingerprints the adapter-induced score inflation described in Luan et al.'s multi-vector retrieval analysis, since high variance is the geometric signature of a poorly calibrated adapter projecting into an unfamiliar region. These three signals — provenance ratio deviation, inter-partition score gap, and variance ratio — can be combined into a single incommensurability score via a lightweight logistic regression trained on synthetic perturbations of a clean index, producing a per-query corruption probability that gates a fallback to v2-only retrieval or triggers cross-encoder re-ranking of the merged candidates. Systems like Vespa already expose the infrastructure to attach per-hit metadata and compute query-level aggregates in the same serving pass, meaning this detection adds roughly 1–2ms of latency overhead — the operational barrier is not compute but instrumentation discipline, since most teams never log partition provenance at the hit level.

The fundamental problem is that a drifting mix ratio invalidates the null distribution that the binomial provenance test and inter-partition gap detector are calibrated against — if the index ingests 10,000 v2-native documents per hour while v1 vectors are being lazily re-encoded, the true mix ratio shifts continuously and a detector calibrated on yesterday's 40% stale baseline will fire false alarms today when staleness has dropped to 25%, eroding operator trust and causing alert fatigue that masks genuine corruption events. The correct framing is to treat the mix ratio as a latent variable to be tracked online rather than a fixed reference: maintain a lightweight count of v1 vs. v2 vectors as a side-channel updated at ingestion time (an O(1) atomic counter increment per document write), and recompute the null proportion for the binomial test per-query using the instantaneous counter values — this makes the provenance ratio detector self-calibrating with zero additional inference cost and eliminates the calibration window entirely for that signal. The inter-partition score gap and variance ratio detectors are harder because they require a reference score distribution, not just a count: the principled solution is an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) of the per-query gap statistic with a half-life tuned to the index update rate (e.g., half-life of 1 hour for an index ingesting thousands of documents per hour), which tracks the drifting baseline without storing the full history, analogous to how CUSUM control charts detect process mean shifts in streaming quality control settings. When the mix ratio drifts faster than the EWMA half-life, the detector enters a regime where the smoothed baseline lags the true distribution — this manifests not as false alarms but as detector blindness: the gap statistic appears near-zero because both the reference and the current observation are shifting together, exactly the failure mode that makes silent corruption undetectable; the signature of this regime is anomalously low variance in the EWMA signal, which is itself a meta-detector trigger. The operational solution used in high-velocity search systems (e.g., Elasticsearch's segment-level metadata) is to stratify the EWMA by index segment age: maintain separate running statistics for documents ingested in the last 1h, 1–24h, and 24h+ windows, so that fresh-segment and stale-segment score distributions are tracked independently, allowing the detector to identify whether corruption is concentrated in a specific ingestion cohort rather than being averaged away across the full corpus.

The cleanest index-external anchor is a frozen sentinel corpus: a small set of documents (100–500 is sufficient) that are re-encoded by every new encoder version at deployment time, never updated, and stored outside the live index in a separate immutable store — because these sentinels are always re-encoded fresh by the current query encoder, their score distribution against a fixed query probe set represents the true v2-native baseline geometry, and any divergence between sentinel scores and live-index scores for the same queries directly measures accumulated drift without touching ingestion metadata. The sentinel query set should be drawn from historical query logs stratified by topic cluster (k-means over query embeddings, one probe per cluster centroid) so that the re-grounding signal covers the full query manifold rather than a biased sample — this is essentially the same design as the "canary queries" used in Google's search quality evaluation infrastructure, where a fixed evaluation set is scored against every index change to detect ranking regressions. A structurally different external anchor is user interaction signals decoupled from retrieval scores: click-through rate, dwell time, or explicit feedback on retrieved documents reflects true relevance as perceived by users independently of what the index computed, and a sudden decorrelation between CTR rank and retrieval rank (measurable as a drop in Spearman ρ between score-rank and CTR-rank for the same query-document pairs) is a ground-truth signal that score distributions have become miscalibrated without requiring any labels. The sentinel corpus approach re-grounds the baseline at a cadence decoupled from ingestion — for example, running sentinel probes every 15 minutes on a cron schedule independent of document write volume — so that even if the ingestion pipeline is writing 50,000 documents per hour and the EWMA is blind, the sentinel signal fires on a fixed clock and provides an absolute reference point; the cost is roughly O(|sentinels| × |probe queries|) dot products per probe cycle, which for 500 sentinels and 200 probes is 100,000 dot products — microseconds on any modern ANNS system. The key design requirement is that sentinels must be semantically stable documents — reference texts whose meaning does not change over time (e.g., encyclopedia-style definitions, canonical FAQ entries) — because if sentinel content drifts in meaning, their score distribution shifts for semantic rather than geometric reasons, confounding the re-grounding signal with content change; this requirement rules out news articles or product descriptions as sentinels and points toward curated, version-controlled reference documents maintained outside any content management pipeline.
